d: Learn how to navigate the Linux file system using basic navigation commands. By the end of this lab, you should be able to identify your current location,…
Learn how to create, organize, copy, rename, move, and delete files and directories in Kali Linux. These skills are essential for managing project files,…
Learn how to view the contents of files and locate files within the Linux file system. These skills are essential for reading configuration files,…
Learn how Linux file permissions work and how to modify them using the `chmod` command. By the end of this lab, you will understand who can read, write, and…
Understand what footprinting is, why attackers and penetration testers perform it, and the difference between passive and active reconnaissance.
Retrieve domain registration information — registrar, registration and expiry dates, name servers, and registrant contact details — to map an organization's…
Discover DNS records and understand their purpose — A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, and CNAME records — to map a domain's infrastructure.
Identify the technologies powering a website — web server, CMS, programming language, frameworks, and JavaScript libraries — using WhatWeb and manual…
Understand how websites expose or restrict crawler access via robots.txt, and use it to uncover hidden directories a site doesn't want indexed.
Use advanced Google search operators for OSINT — site:, filetype:, intitle:, inurl:, and cache: — to surface information the target never intended to publish.
Identify publicly exposed email addresses and subdomains using theHarvester, expanding the target's attack surface through passive sources.
Gather IP-level information about a target using ping and traceroute — connectivity, latency, and the routing path packets take across the internet.
Discover live hosts on a network using nmap -sn — ICMP ping sweep, ARP discovery on local links, and the "host is up" report — building the list of targets…

Retrieve service banners to identify software versions using nc, telnet, and curl — an active technique that confirms exactly what version of software is…
Combine every technique from the path into one authorized engagement: WHOIS, DNS enumeration, website fingerprinting, robots.txt analysis, subdomain…
Learn what network scanning is, the TCP three-way handshake, the common scan types, and the structured CEH network-scanning methodology.
Scan the Globex target with Nmap to enumerate exactly which TCP ports are open and which are closed or filtered.
Identify the exact software and version behind each open port using Nmap service/version detection.
Determine the operating system behind the target using Nmap OS detection and TCP/IP stack analysis.
Explore NULL, FIN, Xmas and ACK scans, how the Linux stack replies to each, and why these 'stealth' techniques matter.
Learn how to turn Nmap's evasion knobs — fragmentation, decoys, timing and source-port spoofing — and what they do to detection.
Use Nmap's Scripting Engine to look for known weaknesses, misconfigurations and outdated services before any exploit phase.
Capstone: run the complete scanning methodology against the Globex host — host discovery, full port sweep, versions, OS — and hunt down the hidden flag.
Learn the purpose of enumeration, then discover the Globex SMB file shares with smbclient and enum4linux.
Stay in the Samba shares: harvest credentials from the misconfigured public share, then map what they unlock.
Probe the SNMP agent on UDP 161, compare community strings, and walk the MIB tree to enumerate the appliance.
Bind anonymously to the OpenLDAP directory and walk the Globex tree: users, groups, mail attributes and service accounts.
Enumerate the portmapper, identify NFS programs, list exports with showmount, and read files from the open share.
Grab service banners across the appliance and use SMTP VRFY/EXPN to confirm which usernames exist.
Identify the KDC on TCP 88 and recover the full set of Kerberos principals with nmap's krb5-enum-users script.
Capstone: run the full enumeration methodology on the Globex appliance and pivot from an anonymous share to the restricted IT archive to capture the flag.
Learn what a vulnerability assessment is, how it differs from a penetration test, and the six-phase vulnerability management lifecycle.
Score real findings with the CVSS v3.1 base metric groups and understand how severity becomes a remediation priority.
Turn service banners into CVE leads: version the target, map findings with searchsploit/Exploit-DB, and check nmap's vulners feed.
Run nmap's vuln/vulners script battery against the appliance and learn to separate real findings from false positives.
Point Nikto at the Globex web server and record the findings: exposed directories, tech-stack leakage and missing security headers.
Audit the appliance for the classic default-misconfig set: guest shares, anonymous FTP, open SNMP, anonymous LDAP and world-readable NFS exports.
Check the appliance for default/weak authentication: default SNMP community strings and credential pairs that should never be reused on corporate shares.
Run the complete assessment: automated vuln scans, web scans, version/exploit research, and a misconfiguration audit — then produce the headline finding.
Understand web-application exploitation: the HTTP request/response cycle, parameters, sessions and the flaw classes (OWASP Top 10) this phase attacks.
Break into the Globex portal without valid credentials: inject a tautology into the login query to bypass authentication completely.
Turn the dashboard search into a data-extraction engine: use a UNION-based injection to dump the users table, including the admin's password.
Store a script payload in the public feedback board and watch it execute in the context of the app: stored XSS with real consequences.
Smuggle operating-system commands through a ping utility in the web app: chain a command separator and read the server's flag file.
Convince the file-viewer page to read outside its sandbox: climb directories with ../ and disclose the server's flag file.
Read another user's private notes by changing a client-supplied object id: surface a broken-access-control flaw (OWASP A01).
Chain the whole web exploitation methodology: authenticate to the file-sharing portal, upload a disguised shell script, and execute it for server control.
Understand what happens after the initial foothold: privilege escalation, persistence, lateral movement and cleaning up your tracks.
Systematically enumerate a Linux host from an unprivileged shell: users, sudo rules, SUID binaries, cron jobs and kernel — the material every privesc report…
Locate the SUID-stick binary the Globex admins left behind and run it — it executes with root privileges and prints data only root may read.
Exploit an over-generous sudo rule: the globex user can run vim as root with no password — escape to a root shell with a GTFOBins one-liner.
Find the root-scheduled backup script that is writable by everyone, swap in your own command, and wait for root to execute it for you.
Turn your temporary root shell into durable access: install your public key into root's authorized_keys and log straight in as root — no password, no…
Pivot from the compromised app host to the internal DC server using the same corporate password — the credential-reuse finding from your vulnerability…
Reduce your forensic footprint: blank shell history, remove authored files, trim auth logs and normalise file timestamps before you leave the host.
A lost-drive binary is suspected malware. Analyse it safely: static triage, hash-based threat-intel lookup and controlled dynamic execution to classify it.
